title: “Optimal tariffs” are far from optimal: Part 1
gist: Two PIIE economists dismantle the Trump administration's "optimal tariff" justification, arguing US terms of trade have not improved since 2025 and that US consumers and firms bear nearly the full tariff cost. They argue corporate tax reform would raise roughly $4 trillion over 2030-2039 (about twice the Trump tariff regime's projected revenue) while shifting more burden onto foreigners, who own 42 percent of US corporate equity.

themes.theme: Why the optimal-tariff argument fails in practice

insights.claim: The 'optimal tariff' argument holds that a large country can raise national welfare by using tariffs to cut import demand and expand domestic supply, thereby driving down the world price of its imports and improving its terms of trade — but this theoretical result does not survive contact with the real world.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The intellectual foundation for continued US tariff escalation is weaker than officials claim; expect the policy to be defended on political rather than economic grounds and to be vulnerable to reversal.
insights.quote: the "optimal tariff" maximizes national welfare by enabling large countries to improve their terms of trade
insights.locator: Problems with the "optimal tariff"

insights.claim: Not every large country can pursue an optimal-tariff strategy simultaneously: the relative price effects cancel out, leaving only universal distortions and no gains from trade.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: As more countries copy US tariff tactics, the global outcome is pure deadweight loss — a structural drag on world trade volumes rather than a zero-sum transfer.
insights.quote: the relative price effects would cancel out, leaving only universal distortions with no gains from trade
insights.locator: However, there are multiple serious, even fatal, problems

insights.claim: Tariff-driven beggar-thy-neighbor dynamics worsened the Great Depression, and preventing a repeat was a crucial motive behind the design of the postwar world trading system.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Historical precedent argues the tail risk from broad tariff escalation is a systemic contraction in trade, not a manageable revenue trade-off.
insights.quote: preventing a repeat was a crucial motive behind the design of the world trading system
insights.locator: Indeed, the foolishness of these sorts of tariffs

insights.claim: In the textbook optimal-tariff decomposition, the government revenue effect is generally the largest of the three welfare channels, so moderate and declining US tariff revenue is itself direct evidence that the optimal-tariff case is failing.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Tariff receipts are the cleanest single indicator to monitor: falling revenue simultaneously undercuts the fiscal and the welfare case for the policy.
insights.quote: Because the largest of these effects is generally the government revenue effect, the fact that US tariff revenue has been moderate and declining is another indication of the limits of the optimal tariff argument.

themes.theme: Retaliation and trade diversion erode US terms of trade

insights.claim: China successfully pursued tit-for-tat retaliation against US tariffs, including export controls, until the US backed down; Canada, Brazil, and the EU also mounted episodes of retaliation.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Export controls are the demonstrated effective counter-lever; sectors dependent on Chinese-controlled inputs carry asymmetric policy risk.
insights.quote: with the notable exception of China, which successfully pursued a tit-for-tat retaliation (including export controls) until the US backed down
insights.locator: A possible response would be that the US has not experienced

insights.claim: Even without explicit retaliation, foreign governments degrade US terms of trade by rearranging trade relationships — the EU struck new trade agreements with India and Mercosur, and Canada has sought to expand trade with China and others in the wake of US trade policy shifts.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The durable damage is quiet market-access diversion away from US exporters; watch EU-India and EU-Mercosur implementation as a leading indicator of US export share loss.
insights.quote: These sorts of policy changes also drive down demand for US exports, harming the US terms of trade.
insights.locator: However, it is not just explicit retaliation

insights.claim: Export controls or export taxes can worsen a target country's terms of trade by making its import goods more expensive or harder to acquire — a symmetric weapon to tariffs.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Terms-of-trade warfare is not limited to import duties; supply-chain chokepoint exposure deserves the same risk weighting as tariff exposure.
insights.quote: Export controls or export taxes can also worsen the target countries' terms of trade, by making their import goods more expensive and/or difficult to acquire.
insights.locator: 3. Export controls or export taxes

themes.theme: The empirical record: no terms-of-trade gain, full domestic pass-through

insights.claim: Through the first quarter of 2026, aggregate US terms-of-trade data showed little improvement despite Trump raising tariffs on almost all imports beginning in early 2025.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The core empirical promise of the tariff program has not materialized after roughly 18 months — a falsification investors can track in published terms-of-trade series.
insights.quote: Until the second quarter of 2026, the data indicated little improvement in the aggregate US terms of trade after Trump began his second term in early 2025 and increased tariffs on almost all imports
insights.locator: Until the second quarter of 2026, the data indicated

insights.claim: The very recent US terms-of-trade improvement is more plausibly attributable to wartime disruptions than to tariffs, and far larger terms-of-trade movements occurred in the wake of COVID-19.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Do not read the recent print as tariff validation; the confound is a wartime shock, so the improvement should reverse when that disruption fades.
insights.quote: the very recent US terms of trade improvement is more plausibly related to wartime disruptions than to tariffs, which have fluctuated considerably
insights.locator: Multiple factors besides tariffs

insights.claim: A preponderance of high-quality research finds US consumers and firms are paying nearly the full cost of US tariffs, meaning America has limited ability to shift net tax burdens onto foreigners through tariffs.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Model tariffs as a domestic consumption tax hitting US corporate margins and household real income, not as a foreign-funded revenue windfall.
insights.quote: A preponderance of high-quality research studies shows that US consumers and firms are paying nearly the full cost of US tariffs

insights.claim: More detailed econometric studies fail to reveal any major effect of tariffs on the terms of trade.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The pass-through-to-foreigners assumption embedded in official revenue forecasts is not empirically supported, implying downside risk to those forecasts.

themes.theme: Tariff revenue fragility and legal risk

insights.claim: US tariff revenues turned negative in June 2026 for the first time, as government refunds of the 'reciprocal' tariffs deemed illegal by the Supreme Court exceeded new tariff collections.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: A concrete fiscal hole and a refund windfall for importers — screen for companies with large accrued tariff payments eligible for recovery.
insights.quote: Tariff revenues even turned negative in June 2026 for the first time as government refunds of Trump's so-called reciprocal tariffs—deemed illegal by the Supreme Court—exceeded new tariff revenues
insights.locator: And revenues from the Trump tariffs are also highly uncertain

insights.claim: Revenues from the Trump tariffs are highly uncertain because of persistent legal challenges to the tariff regimes.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Tariff-linked fiscal projections carry unusual variance; litigation outcomes are a discrete catalyst for both the deficit path and importer cash flows.
insights.locator: And revenues from the Trump tariffs are also highly uncertain

insights.claim: Latest estimates imply the Trump tariff regime raises about half (or perhaps less) of the roughly $4 trillion that a package of corporate tax reforms is projected to raise over the coming decade.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: If the fiscal rationale is the binding constraint, corporate tax increases are the natural substitute — a tail risk for US corporate earnings if tariffs are struck down.
insights.quote: The latest estimates of the Trump tariff regime imply revenues of about half that (or perhaps less) over the coming decade
insights.locator: Corporate tax reform can also raise a lot of revenue

themes.theme: Corporate tax reform as the superior instrument

insights.claim: Foreigners hold 42 percent of US corporate equity (2022 data, direct and indirect holdings), so the corporate income tax shifts tax burden onto foreigners far more effectively than tariffs do.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The strongest policy substitute for tariffs falls directly on equity holders — a direct valuation risk to US-listed corporates held by global investors.
insights.quote: The corporate income tax can do that very well, since 42 percent of US corporate equity is held by foreigners
insights.locator: There are better tax instruments

insights.claim: The Penn-Wharton Budget Model estimates the Clausing (2026) package of corporate tax reforms would raise $4 trillion over 2030-2039, about 0.9 percent of GDP.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: A quantified, scored alternative revenue plan already exists — raising the probability it becomes the policy of a future administration.
insights.quote: raises $4 trillion over 2030-2039, or about 0.9 percent of GDP
insights.locator: Corporate tax reform can also raise a lot of revenue

insights.claim: The US corporate tax system contains a large tax preference for foreign income relative to domestic income, so low-tax destinations attract a great deal of the US multinational corporate tax base — making corporate tax reform a better answer to offshoring than tariffs.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Multinationals with heavy low-tax-jurisdiction income booking face the concentrated downside if this reform path is adopted.
insights.quote: The US corporate tax system includes a large tax preference for foreign income relative to domestic income.
insights.locator: At the same time, corporate tax reform can be a better response

insights.claim: Tariffs shift resources toward sectors where the US lacks a comparative advantage while introducing new distortions that hurt consumers.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Capacity built behind tariff walls in non-comparative-advantage sectors is stranded-asset risk if the tariff regime is unwound by courts or a new administration.
insights.quote: tariffs introduce new distortions that hurt consumers and shift resources toward sectors where the US lacks a comparative advantage
insights.locator: In contrast, tariffs introduce new distortions

insights.claim: Corporate taxes are among the most progressive US tax instruments beyond the estate tax, whereas tariffs are regressive, taking more from lower-income households as a share of income than from well-off households.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: The distributional politics of tariffs are a persistent vulnerability — expect low-income consumer spending pressure and eventual political backlash.
insights.locator: A final consideration is having a tax system

insights.claim: Beyond corporate taxes, individual tax reforms or new instruments such as a carbon tax could replace tariff revenue more efficiently, given that the tariff regime burdens consumers and businesses, generates large distortions, harms international relations, and provides rampant opportunities for corruption and rent-seeking.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Clausing, Maurice Obstfeld
insights.so_what: Carbon tax optionality re-enters the US fiscal conversation as a tariff replacement — relevant to energy-intensive sectors and carbon-pricing exposure.
insights.quote: provides rampant opportunities for corruption and rent-seeking
